title: Planetary Information Processing and Memory Storage Through Deep Time: A Bounded Order-of-Magnitude Reconstruction from Prebiotic Chemistry to the Modern Technosphere
plain_title: Counting a planet's memory and computing
thesis: Count everything on Earth that stores or processes information, from the first cells to today's data centers, keep each kind in its own units, and four findings stand out.
summary: The paper builds a census of Earth at 64 moments over 4.1 billion years. At each moment it estimates ten separate quantities: three kinds of DNA storage, two kinds of memory, three kinds of event rate (cell chemistry, nerve signals, chip operations), total power, and how long information persists. Today's values are built from published counts of cells, animals and devices, with uncertainty ranges from 10,000 random draws. Older values are scaled back from those anchors using fossils and rock chemistry.

claims.claim: Life and technology together use a fixed, countable amount of power.
claims.paper_value: 65.0 TW for life plus 19.5 TW for technology, 84.5 TW in all
claims.note: The six compartments in the ledger sum to the stated totals.

claims.claim: Life uses about half of what plants capture from sunlight.
claims.source: Census value for life's power; the 125 TW figure is cited from outside literature
claims.note: The division is right; the 125 TW anchor itself is not in the project's data.

claims.claim: Microbial power divides into deep-underground, standby and active cells.
claims.paper_value: 0.69 TW, 3.89 TW and 9.42 TW, totalling 14.00 TW (corrected 9 Nov 2026; first version said 0.69 GW and 10.11 TW)
claims.data_value: 0.69 TW, 3.89 TW and 9.42 TW, totalling 14.00 TW
claims.note: Corrected on 9 November 2026: the abstract, section 2.4 and the appendix now give the ledger's values, which add up to 14.00 TW.

claims.claim: The number of microbial cells follows from their total carbon.
claims.paper_value: 3.10×10³⁰ cells from 77.5 billion tonnes of carbon at 25 femtograms per cell
claims.source: Census: microbial carbon divided by carbon per cell

claims.claim: Cell chemistry is the largest event rate on the planet.
claims.paper_value: 2.80×10³³ events a second, 95% range 9.46×10³² to 8.25×10³³ (corrected 9 Nov 2026)
claims.note: Corrected on 9 November 2026: the abstract now quotes the range from the paper's own uncertainty table. That table's central value, 2.70×10³³, is slightly below the census's 2.80×10³³.

claims.claim: All the DNA in living cells can be counted in bits.
claims.paper_value: 3.60×10³⁷ bits in total, 1.84×10³⁷ under selection, 3.80×10¹² unique
claims.note: All three values are in the census as stated.

claims.claim: Every animal nervous system together fires a countable number of signals.
claims.paper_value: 3.43×10²⁴ neurons, 3.00×10²⁷ synapses, 3.00×10²⁶ signals a second, 95% range 9.08×10²⁵ to 9.92×10²⁶ (corrected 9 Nov 2026)
claims.data_value: 3.43×10²⁴ neurons, 3.00×10²⁷ synapses, 3.00×10²⁶ signals a second (95% range 0.9×10²⁶ to 9.9×10²⁶)
claims.source: Census; synapses × 0.10 signals a second each; uncertainty ledger
claims.note: Corrected on 9 November 2026: the range now comes from the uncertainty table; the earlier 1.5 to 8.5×10²⁶ is kept and labelled as a firing-rate band.

claims.claim: Two mass extinctions each removed more than nine tenths of nerve signalling.
claims.paper_value: 94% at the end of the Permian, 92.5% at the asteroid impact
claims.source: Census: change between the moments either side of each extinction; uncertainty ledger
claims.note: Both drops recompute exactly from the census. They are constrained scenarios, not measurements.

claims.claim: All the world's chips together execute a countable number of operations.
claims.paper_value: 1.89×10²² operations a second, 9.00×10²¹ of them on AI accelerators, drawing 80 GW
claims.data_value: 1.89×10²² operations a second, 9.00×10²¹ on AI accelerators, 80 GW
claims.note: Totals match, and 15 million accelerators × 10¹⁵ operations × 60% use gives 9.0×10²¹. Corrected on 9 November 2026: the abstract now splits the rest the way the device ledger does.

claims.claim: Chips remain far below nervous systems when everything is added up.
claims.paper_value: about 15,900 times below all animals and 65 times below all human brains
claims.source: Census: nerve signals ÷ chip operations; 8.2 billion people × 1.5×10¹⁴ signals each ÷ chip operations
claims.note: Both ratios recompute. The census's own population figure is 8.1 billion, which gives 64.

claims.claim: One large AI cluster out-runs one human brain.
claims.paper_value: 3.00×10²⁰ operations against 1.50×10¹⁴ signals a second: 2 million times
claims.source: Census: largest single system today ÷ one human brain
claims.note: The division is right. It compares chip operations with nerve signals, which are different kinds of event.

claims.claim: Modern storage holds a great deal but would not last long unpowered.
claims.paper_value: 1.20×10²³ bits installed; 9.96×10²³ bit-years unpowered; mean lifetimes 3.5 years flash, 7.0 hard disks, 25 tape; 20 GW of refresh power, 9 GW of it for storage (corrected 9 Nov 2026)
claims.data_value: Memory ledger: the same values. The census row for 2026 carries 4.2×10²³ bit-years instead of 9.96×10²³.
claims.note: Corrected on 9 November 2026: lifetimes, labels and the split of the 20 GW now follow the memory ledger. One difference remains, in the project's data rather than the paper: the census and the ledger disagree on unpowered persistence.

claims.claim: The reconstruction is calibrated on a large catalog of systems.
claims.source: Catalog workbook: distinct ids counted on the Systems, Measurements and Sources sheets
claims.note: The catalog has grown by 25 systems, 25 measurements and 25 sources since the paper was written. The paper's counts describe the catalog it used, so they were left as they are.

rationale.step: Keep ten quantities in their own units and never merge them into one score.
rationale.note: The paper does this throughout; bits, events a second, watts and bit-years are never added together.

rationale.step: Build today's values bottom-up from published counts and require the pieces to add up.
rationale.note: Carbon to cells to power closes exactly in the ledgers, and the totals recompute.

rationale.step: Scale back through deep time from today's anchors using fossils, rock chemistry and living relatives.
rationale.note: There is no other way to do it, and the paper labels these moments as scenarios, but values before the modern inventory cannot be tested and carry wide ranges.

rationale.step: Compare cell chemistry, nerve signals and chip operations by counting events a second.
rationale.note: The counts are sound, but one reaction, one nerve signal and one chip operation are not equal amounts of work, as the paper itself says. The ratios say how often, not how much thinking.

rationale.step: Carry uncertainty through with 10,000 random draws.
rationale.note: The ledger has the ranges, though the abstract quotes narrower ones for two quantities.

conclusions.conclusion: The world's chips have not overtaken the world's nervous systems.
conclusions.note: The joint 95% range of the chip-to-nerve ratio runs from 1.6×10⁻⁵ to 2.3×10⁻⁴, so it stays far below 1 across the whole range.

conclusions.conclusion: One frontier AI cluster exceeds one human brain by six orders of magnitude.
conclusions.note: The arithmetic is right. Read as raw event counts it holds; read as a statement about capability it does not follow, because the events differ.

conclusions.conclusion: Mass extinctions acted as resets that cleared small-brained incumbents and released the rise of mammals and birds.
conclusions.note: The size of the drops is a model scenario with wide ranges, and the paper does not test the causal step from clearing to release.

conclusions.conclusion: Digital storage needs continuous power to avoid being erased.
conclusions.note: After the 9 November correction the paper says that of the 20 GW refresh power, 9 GW keeps storage from being erased and 11 GW refreshes working memory, which matches its ledger.

inconsistencies: Section 2.4 gives each group of microbes its own carbon per cell and event rate (for example 100 transitions a second for deep microbes), while Table B1 uses a uniform 25 femtograms of carbon per cell and different rates. Both give the same totals.
The uncertainty table's central values (2.70×10³³, 3.02×10²⁶, 1.87×10²²) differ slightly from the census (2.80×10³³, 3.00×10²⁶, 1.89×10²²).
The census and the memory ledger give different unpowered persistence for outside memory (4.2×10²³ against 9.96×10²³ bit-years); the paper follows the ledger.
The world population is 8.2 billion in the text and 8.1 billion in the census.
Figures 1 to 3 were drawn before the correction and still label the 1.5 to 8.5×10²⁶ band as the uncertainty of nerve signalling.
bottom_line: After the 9 November correction, today’s totals, the ratios between them, the uncertainty ranges and the extinction drops all agree with the paper’s ledgers and can be relied on as order-of-magnitude estimates. The deep-time values and the causal story about extinctions remain scenarios, and five smaller differences between the text, its tables and the project’s data are left for the authors.
revised: On 9 November 2026, after this check, six errors in the abstract and body (a wrong unit, a value that broke the power budget, two uncertainty ranges, a device breakdown, memory lifetimes and the use of 20 GW of refresh power) were corrected to match the paper’s own tables. The original is kept as a backup.
